questions.question: What is the OWASP API Security Top 10?

options.text: A list of the most critical API security risks

questions.explanation: OWASP API Security Top 10 identifies critical API vulnerabilities: Broken Object Level Authorization, Broken Authentication, Excessive Data Exposure, etc. Essential reading for API security.

questions.question: What is Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA)?

options.text: When APIs don't verify users can access the specific objects they request

questions.explanation: BOLA (IDOR) occurs when APIs accept object IDs without verifying the user has permission. Example: GET /api/users/123/data - does the requester have access to user 123's data? Always verify authorization.

questions.question: Which practices help prevent injection attacks in APIs? (Choose all that apply)
questions.explanation: Parameterized queries prevent SQL injection. Input validation rejects malicious input. Output escaping prevents XSS. String concatenation for queries is the CAUSE of injection vulnerabilities.

questions.question: What is the principle of least privilege in API design?

options.text: Give all users admin access for convenience
Grant only the minimum permissions necessary for a task

questions.explanation: Least privilege means users/services get only permissions they need. API tokens should have minimal scopes. This limits damage from compromised credentials and reduces attack surface.

questions.question: Why should API error messages be carefully designed?

options.text: Detailed errors can leak sensitive information to attackers

questions.explanation: Verbose errors can reveal stack traces, database schemas, internal paths, or valid usernames. Return generic errors to clients; log details server-side. Example: 'Invalid credentials' not 'User not found'.

questions.question: What is API rate limiting's role in security?

options.text: It only affects performance, not security
It prevents brute force attacks, DoS, and resource exhaustion

questions.explanation: Rate limiting prevents: brute force password attacks, credential stuffing, DoS attacks, and scraping. It's a critical security control, not just performance optimization.

questions.question: True or False: HTTPS alone is sufficient for API security.
questions.explanation: HTTPS provides transport security (encryption in transit) but doesn't address authentication, authorization, input validation, rate limiting, or application-level vulnerabilities. It's necessary but not sufficient.

questions.question: What is 'Excessive Data Exposure' in API security?

options.text: APIs returning more data than the client needs, relying on client-side filtering

questions.explanation: APIs often return full objects, expecting clients to filter. Attackers can see all data in responses. APIs should return only necessary fields. Don't rely on client-side filtering for security.

questions.question: How should API keys be protected?

options.text: Store in environment variables, never commit to code repositories
Include them in URLs for easy access

questions.explanation: API keys should be in environment variables or secret managers, never in code/repos. Use .gitignore for config files. Rotate keys regularly. Use different keys for dev/prod environments.

questions.question: What is CORS and why is it important for API security?

options.text: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing - controls which domains can access your API from browsers

questions.explanation: CORS headers control browser cross-origin requests. Misconfigured CORS (Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *) can allow malicious sites to make authenticated requests to your API using victim's cookies.

questions.question: What security headers should APIs include? (Choose all that apply)
questions.explanation: Security headers: CSP (prevents XSS), X-Content-Type-Options (prevents MIME sniffing), HSTS (enforces HTTPS), X-Frame-Options (prevents clickjacking). X-API-Speed is not a real header.

questions.question: An API endpoint allows users to update their profile. What authorization check is essential?

options.text: Check if the user is logged in
Verify the user can only update their OWN profile, not others'
Check if the request uses HTTPS

questions.explanation: Authentication (logged in) isn't enough. Authorization must verify the user can access/modify the specific resource. PUT /users/123 should verify the requester IS user 123 or has admin rights.
